summary: <strong>Background:</strong> AI-enabled patient profiling has been proposed to organize heterogeneous patient data and support personalized nursing care and health support. Given the growing use of AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), digital phenotyping, and digital twins in health care, it is important to clarify how patient profiling has been conceptualized, applied, and evaluated in nursing-relevant contexts. <strong>Objective:</strong> This scoping review aimed to examine and report the available evidence on AI-enabled patient profiling for personalized nursing care and health support. <strong>Methods:</strong> This scoping review was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews). Chinese and English databases were searched from inception to May 18, 2026, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Embase. Eligible studies used AI or computational intelligence methods to construct, classify, apply, validate, or evaluate patient profiles or related patient representations relevant to personalized nursing care or health support. Two reviewers independently screened records, assessed full texts, and charted data using a predefined form. Data were synthesized descriptively and narratively using an input-process-output framework. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 61 studies were included. AI-enabled patient profiling was represented through patient profiles, patient or user personas, digital phenotypes, patient segments, clinical subtypes, digital twins, and LLM-enabled personalization. Included studies used diverse data sources, including electronic health records, nursing records, patient-reported outcomes, questionnaires, mobile app data, wearable and sensor data, engagement logs, and textual or conversational data. Common AI approaches included machine learning, clustering, deep learning, natural language processing, recommender systems, knowledge graphs, digital twin modeling, and LLMs. Applications focused on personalized education, self-management support, rehabilitation, chronic disease management, remote monitoring, decision support, follow-up care, and shared decision-making. Most studies evaluated algorithmic performance, feasibility, usability, or system development, whereas fewer studies examined profile validity, actionability, equity, workflow integration, or long-term nursing-sensitive and patient-centered outcomes. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Existing evidence positions AI-enabled patient profiling as an emerging data-to-action mechanism for personalized nursing care and health support rather than as a mature clinical intervention. Future research should strengthen conceptual clarity, validate the profile, establish explicit pathways linking profiles to actions, incorporate nurse and patient involvement, assess equity and safety, and evaluate implementation in real-world nursing settings. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> OSF Registry mey4u; https://osf.io/mey4u
title: AI-Enabled Patient Profiling for Personalized Nursing Care and Health Support: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Emerging evidence indicates that immersive virtual reality can be used therapeutically and has demonstrated efficacy in promoting the mental health of older adults. Nevertheless, there remains a paucity of qualitative research examining the specific experiences underpinning these benefits. Objective: This study aimed to explore the perspectives of older adults who received the 12-session Immersive Virtual Reality Therapeutic Programme (IVRTP) intervention and health-related undergraduate students who delivered it as interventionists, within the context of residential care homes. Methods: A descriptive qualitative study was conducted as a qualitative exploration embedded in a multicenter randomized controlled trial evaluating the effects of IVRTP in promoting the mental health of older adults with disabilities living in residential homes. The IVRTP incorporated therapeutic elements of tourism, natural scenes, and reminiscence. Data were collected through focus group interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Results: Seven groups of older adults (n=28) and 3 groups of student interventionists (n=9) participated in the study. Five themes emerged: IVRTP contributes to “broadening horizons” through embracing new technology, learning new things, and engaging in new activities. Participants noted that the IVRTP provided “a realistic journey and immersive escape” from their residential home environment and mobility issues. They expressed that the IVRTP evoked “reminiscent memories” from the past and were amazed at the observed changes in tourist destinations over time. The interviews were filled with laughter and affirmations of positive emotions associated with this “joyful adventure,” although a few participants mentioned “minor discomfort,” such as eye soreness and dizziness, from wearing the head-mounted devices. Students’ accounts corroborated these themes; their meaning-making and colearning with older adults underscored the pedagogical value of authentic, community-based, intergenerational learning and reinforced the case for integrating a community practicum into the curriculum. Conclusions: Implementing an IVRTP in residential care settings, particularly for older adults with mobility limitations, is positively viewed as an accessible, enjoyable, and beneficial intervention to support psychosocial well-being. Therapeutically oriented content delivered through a structured protocol, coupled with the use of advanced IVR technology, was appreciated by both older adults and student interventionists.
title: Experiences of Immersive Virtual Reality Among Older Adults With Physical Disabilities: Qualitative Process Evaluation of a Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Medication nonadherence remains a major global health challenge, contributing to preventable disease, hospitalizations, and health care costs. Mobile health (mHealth) apps incorporating gamification and financial incentives have shown potential to improve adherence; however, most research has focused on patient perspectives, with limited understanding of how nonpatient stakeholders perceive their feasibility, risks, and implementation. Understanding nonpatient stakeholder perspectives in relation to patient viewpoints is essential for informing future policy development and establishing practical, industry-supported safeguards that protect consumers while enabling innovation. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to explore nonpatient stakeholder perspectives on the use of gamification and financial incentives in mHealth apps for medication adherence and to inform consensus-based design and policy considerations. <strong>Methods:</strong> A study was conducted using a modified virtual nominal group technique (vNGT). Nonpatient stakeholders across health care, industry, and policy sectors in Australia were recruited through purposive and convenience sampling between February and August 2025. Data collection involved a survey capturing demographics and initial perspectives, followed by online focus groups for consensus discussions. Qualitative responses were analyzed using thematic analysis supported by AI-assisted coding. Consensus statements derived from themes were rated during the focus groups. Additional probing prompts were used in the focus groups to encourage further discussion where consensus was not immediately achieved. Results from the focus groups were analyzed using descriptive statistics to summarize consensus ratings and discussions. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 20 participants were included in the study. Nine participants reported having a health care professional background employment exclusively, while 11 reported having employment background across multiple sectors or exclusively outside health care. Six key themes were identified: tailored gamification for adherence, financial incentives as a contested motivator, designing for diversity and inclusion, usability barriers to engagement, trust through data governance, and validated and sustainable innovation. These informed 24 consensus statements, of which 54% (13/24) achieved unanimous agreement. Stakeholders strongly endorsed personalization, simplicity, and transparent data practices, while expressing nuanced concerns regarding the ethical use, sustainability, and potential unintended consequences of financial incentives. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Nonpatient stakeholders largely reinforce patient priorities while extending them with critical perspectives on implementation, governance, and sustainability. Gamification and financial incentives are viewed as potentially effective but require careful, ethically grounded design to balance engagement with long-term motivation and trust. These findings support the development of stakeholder-informed guidelines for responsible mHealth innovation and highlight the importance of integrating patient and system-level perspectives in digital health design. Future research should prioritize co-designed longitudinal studies using apps with gamification and a range of incentive offers with clear redemption processes to evaluate the long-term impact on medication adherence across diverse patient populations.
title: Nonpatient Stakeholder Perspectives on the Use of Gamification and Financial Incentives in Mobile Health for Medication Adherence: Modified Nominal Group Technique Study

summary: Meyer-Keirath and colleagues found no significant difference in posttreatment symptoms between video-based and face-to-face psychotherapy. However, the wide confidence interval indicates substantial imprecision, while the prediction interval suggests that comparative effects may vary considerably across settings; neither supports a conclusion of equivalence. For health services, symptom outcomes alone tell only part of the story. Future studies should report, by randomized group, who starts treatment, who discontinues it, and who completes the final assessment. These are distinct outcomes that may differ between delivery formats and affect the interpretation of symptom results. Video-based psychotherapy is a reasonable option, but its value should be assessed across the full treatment pathway. Adequately powered noninferiority trials should identify which patients can access, remain in, and benefit from each format.
title: Supporting Video-Based Psychotherapy While Asking Who Benefits and Who Remains in Treatment

summary: Background: Electronic patient-reported outcomes (ePROs) can support patient-centered oncology care, but in early breast cancer, it is unclear whether real-time ePRO-triggered triage adds benefit beyond lower-intensity app-based support and scheduled ePRO collection. Objective: We tested whether adding weekly ePRO screening, rule-based triage, and care-team escalation to app-based support improves health-related quality of life (HRQoL) during systemic therapy for early breast cancer. Methods: ENABLE was a multicenter, open-label, parallel-group randomized controlled trial at 2 German university hospitals. Adults with early (stage I-III) breast cancer initiating systemic therapy were randomized 1:1 to reactive patient-reported outcome assessment (RPA) or control. Both arms received the ENABLE app with educational and organizational support and scheduled HRQoL assessments at 6 fixed time points; only RPA received weekly EuroQol Visual Analogue Scale screening (trigger: score <50 or ≥10-point decline) followed by symptom assessment, digital triage, and care-team alerts. Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System-29 was analyzed as an 8-measure HRQoL end-point family (7 domains plus pain intensity); no single domain, composite score, or binary global success rule was prespecified. Group-by-visit mixed-effects models were fitted with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate adjustment. The recruitment period was March 22, 2021, to September 8, 2023. Results: Of 605 randomized patients, 487 entered the modified intention-to-treat analysis (RPA: n=242; control: n=245). End-of-treatment between-group differences (RPA minus control, -score points, 95% CI, and adjusted ) were: fatigue −3.90 (95% CI −5.77 to −2.03; =.004), social participation +2.84 (95% CI 1.18 to 4.49; =.01), anxiety −2.10 (95% CI −3.65 to −0.55; =.049), depression −1.95 (95% CI −3.25 to −0.65; =.10), sleep disturbance −1.82 (95% CI −3.43 to −0.20; =.051), pain interference −1.44 (95% CI −3.38 to 0.49; =.18), physical function +1.33 (95% CI −0.22 to 2.88; =.18), and pain intensity −0.26 (95% CI −0.73 to 0.21; =.32; 0‐10 scale). All -score differences were below the 5-point minimally important difference (MID). Exploratory time-to-deterioration analyses favored RPA for fatigue (hazard ratio [HR] 0.69, 95% CI 0.54‐0.89), social participation (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.59-0.97), and depression (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.44-0.98). Of 209 monitored RPA patients, 160 (76.6%; 95% CI 70.4‐81.8) triggered at least 1 alert. No intervention-related harms were identified. Conclusions: ENABLE tests real-time, rule-based ePRO triage with care-team escalation against an active digital comparator rather than usual care, isolating the response pathway itself; it extends this design from metastatic disease into early breast cancer and escalates to the care team rather than to the patient alone. Benefits were domain-specific and sub-MID, in anxiety, fatigue, and social participation, tempering the expectation of a global HRQoL effect. For practice, symptom-triggered triage is a supportive-care workflow tool worth embedding where alerts reach a team that acts and documents, not a stand-alone remedy for treatment-related morbidity. Trial Registration: German Clinical Trials Register DRKS00025611; https://drks.de/search/en/trial/DRKS00025611 International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.2196/69855
title: Real-Time Electronic Patient-Reported Outcome Monitoring With Digital Triage and Care-Team Integration in Early Breast Cancer: ENABLE Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: Background: Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is highly effective for HIV prevention, but its real-world impact depends on sustained adherence. Long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) may reduce the burden of daily or event-driven pill use. In China, many oral PrEP users obtain medication online, but little is known about their prior CAB-LA awareness or willingness to consider it. Objective: This study assessed prior CAB-LA awareness, hypothetical willingness to use CAB-LA, reported barriers and facilitators, and associated factors among oral PrEP users in China obtaining PrEP online. Methods: This cross-sectional study analyzed baseline data from the Real-world E-consumer Cohort of Oral PrEP (RECOPE), a prospective cohort in China. Participants completed a self-administered web-based questionnaire assessing prior CAB-LA awareness, hypothetical willingness after standardized CAB-LA information, sociodemographic characteristics, recent sexual behaviors and sexually transmitted infection (STI) diagnosis, and oral PrEP-related characteristics. Modified Poisson regression with robust SEs estimated prevalence ratios (PRs) and adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) with 95% CIs. Primary regression analyses were restricted to sexually active participants. Results: Among 621 oral PrEP users, the mean age was 29.9 (SD 6.4) years; all were assigned male sex at birth, and 608 (97.9%) identified as men. Overall, 216 of 621 (34.8%, 95% CI 31.1%‐38.6%) participants reported prior CAB-LA awareness. After receiving standardized information, 428 of 621 (68.9%, 95% CI 65.2%‐72.4%) participants expressed hypothetical willingness to use CAB-LA if it became available in China. Convenience was the most frequently reported facilitator among willing participants (395/428, 92.3%), whereas high cost was the most frequently reported barrier among those who did not express willingness (123/193, 63.7%). In adjusted analyses, event-driven PrEP users had a lower prevalence of prior CAB-LA awareness than daily PrEP users (aPR 0.66, 95% CI 0.50‐0.86), whereas participants who had switched oral PrEP regimens in the past 3 months had higher prior awareness (aPR 1.34, 95% CI 1.07‐1.68). Hypothetical willingness was more prevalent among participants reporting an STI diagnosis in the past 3 months (aPR 1.22, 95% CI 1.08‐1.39) and chemsex (aPR 1.13, 95% CI 1.01‐1.26), whereas higher PrEP-related stigma was associated with slightly lower willingness (aPR 0.99 per 1-point increase, 95% CI 0.98‐0.99). Conclusions: Among oral PrEP users in China obtaining PrEP online, prior CAB-LA awareness was limited, whereas hypothetical willingness was common after standardized information was provided. Prior awareness differed by oral PrEP regimen and recent regimen switching, whereas willingness was associated with recent STI diagnosis, chemsex, and PrEP-related stigma. Convenience was a major appeal, while cost remained an important barrier. These findings support improving access to balanced PrEP information and addressing practical barriers as long-acting PrEP becomes more widely available.
title: Awareness of and Hypothetical Willingness to Use Long-Acting Injectable Cabotegravir and Associated Factors Among Oral Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis Users Who Obtained the Medicine Online in China: Web-Based Cross-Sectional Study

summary: In this viewpoint, we present our perspective—informed by published evidence and by our own work on AI-driven digital health systems—on why AI has had limited real-world impact in preventive health and how it should be redesigned. Most AI systems in health care are built as episodic prediction tools, whereas preventive care depends on sustained behavioral change; the consequences are visible in consistently high attrition and low long-term adherence across digital health interventions. The aim of this viewpoint is to argue that this failure is structural rather than incremental and to propose an integrated, interaction-centric alternative. We advance 3 key messages. First, the limited impact of AI in preventive health reflects a structural misalignment between episodic, prediction-centric system design and the longitudinal dynamics of health behavior. Second, addressing this misalignment requires treating continuous interaction as the primary unit of design, which we articulate through a behavioral informatics framework integrating 6 interdependent layers: data, knowledge, reasoning, interaction, behavior, and governance. The contribution of this framework is explicitly integrative: it synthesizes previously separate strands, including just-in-time adaptive interventions, behavioral intervention technologies, and human-AI interaction research, into a single system-level account. Third, evaluation must shift from predictive accuracy and short-term engagement toward measurable behavioral trajectories and longitudinal outcomes, with explicit attention to feasibility and to conditions under which simpler, non-AI interventions remain preferable. This viewpoint is addressed to digital health researchers and AI developers, behavioral scientists, clinicians involved in preventive care, and policymakers responsible for governing continuously interacting AI systems.
title: From Prediction to Interaction: A Behavioral Informatics Framework for AI in Preventive Health

summary: Background: Over 55 million people worldwide are living with dementia, resulting in significant caregiving demands and caregiver burden. Socially assistive robots (SARs) are increasingly being explored to reduce caregiving workload and improve the quality of life for persons with dementia; however, their effectiveness depends on person-centered design grounded in a comprehensive understanding of the target population. Personas and their corresponding daily activity maps (DAMs) are user-centered design tools that provide a holistic understanding of the personal, medical, emotional, and life trajectory of persons with dementia, enabling SARs to engage in contextually relevant and empathetic interactions. Despite their potential, these tools have not been formally evaluated for dementia care and digital health technology development. Objective: This mixed methods study aimed to explore the perspectives of professional and family caregivers, health care providers, and robot designers on the quality and use of personas and DAMs in clinical practice and digital health design. Methods: Using purposive sampling, 15 stakeholders involved in dementia care or digital health design were interviewed via Zoom (Zoom Communications, Inc) between March and April 2025 to evaluate a subset of persona-DAM pairs using a modified 12-item version of the Persona Perception Scale (PPS), adapted for dementia care contexts, across 5 domains: Credibility, Completeness, Clarity, Willingness to Use, and Empathy. Participants subsequently provided qualitative perspectives through semistructured interviews, reflecting on their ratings and offering suggestions for improvement. Results: Fifteen participants with a median of 9 (IQR 4-15) years of experience in dementia care evaluated 9 persona-DAM pairs. Overall evaluation-level median PPS scores were 4.79 (IQR 4.45, 4.91) for personas and 4.76 (IQR 4.45, 4.94) for DAMs. For both personas and DAMs, the highest-rated domains were Clarity, Credibility, and Willingness to Use (all median 5.00), suggesting stakeholders perceived the tools favorably and were willing to use them. Empathy scores (personas: median 4.67, IQR 4.25-5; DAMs: median 4.83, IQR 4.33-5) highlighted the need for greater cultural, ethnic, and religious representation to foster culturally sensitive interventions. Completeness was the lowest-scoring domain (personas: median 4.50, IQR 3.94-5; DAMs: median 4.38, IQR 4-5), representing the most quantitative improvement suggestions. Qualitative analysis revealed 3 major themes: (1) improving human-robot interaction training through greater knowledge of the personal context of persons with dementia; (2) comprehensive assessment of clinical history and functional capacities as essential for the provision of safe and effective interaction; and (3) perceived design utility: translating person-centered knowledge into actionable tools. Conclusions: This study provides early-stage exploratory evidence that personas and DAMs are perceived as clinically and technically relevant tools for dementia care, complementing existing clinical documentation through a holistic, person-centered view, and serving as human-centered design tools for developing personalized digital health solutions. International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.2196/55761
title: Evaluation of Personas and Daily Activity Maps to Inform Clinical Care and Socially Assistive Robot Training and Design for Persons With Dementia: Mixed Methods Study

summary: Background: Generative AI (GenAI) is being deployed rapidly in medicine, and evidence of its clinical safety and efficacy depends on transparent reporting of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The CONSORT-AI (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials–AI) extension is a benchmark for AI trial reporting, but it was drafted for conventional AI, and its applicability to GenAI has not been examined. Objective: This study aimed to assess item-level adherence to the CONSORT-AI among RCTs evaluating GenAI for medical purposes and to distinguish deficiencies attributable to nonadherence from those attributable to items that do not correspond to how GenAI interventions are specified or delivered. Methods: PubMed, CENTRAL (Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials), and Embase were searched for peer-reviewed, English-language RCTs published from 2022 to April 3, 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching, in which patients, health care professionals, or laypeople received a GenAI intervention for a medical purpose; non-GenAI, nonmedical, nonrandomized, and non-peer-reviewed reports were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and rated CONSORT-AI items as reported, partially reported, not reported, or not applicable using signaling questions, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer (Cohen κ=0.81 and prevalence-adjusted, bias-adjusted κ=0.84). Risk of bias was not assessed, as the target was reporting adherence. Adherence was the proportion of reports rated “reported” per item; item-level adherence was compared across 9 characteristics using Fisher exact and Freeman-Halton tests (2-sided α=.05). Results: From 16,485 retrieved records, 74 reports from 73 RCTs (24,150 participants; median 100, IQR 50.0‐247.0) were included. Large language models (LLMs) accounted for 98.6% (73/74) of interventions, with 60.8% (45/74) using GPT-family models. Item-level reporting adherence ranged from 0% (0/72) to 98.6% (73/74). High adherence occurred in general metadata and output specification items (range 59-73, 79.7%‐98.6%). Conversely, reporting was poor for input and technical execution domains, input data eligibility (3/73, 4.1%), input acquisition/selection (9/74, 12.2%), algorithm versioning (17/74, 23.0%), trial setting integration (21/74, 28.4%), human-AI interaction (25/74, 33.8%), performance error (27/74, 36.5%), and open access/code (31/74, 41.9%). Input quality handling (Item 5[iii]) was completely unreported (0/72). Only 9 of 74 (12.2%) reports explicitly cited CONSORT-AI. While citing reports showed higher compliance for interaction and data sharing, major technical gaps persisted regardless of citation. Conclusions: This review provides the first empirical audit distinguishing general nonadherence from structural mismatches where deterministic CONSORT-AI items fail to capture GenAI mechanics. Differing from traditional AI evaluations, it reveals that key reproducibility drivers—system prompts, inference settings, and access modalities—are omitted from current standards. These empirical findings highlight critical reporting gaps in medical GenAI trials and identify domains for a tailored extension to current reporting standards, although the evidence is limited by the use of nonvalidated signaling questions. Establishing GenAI-specific trial guidelines will ensure that clinical decisions, regulatory approvals, and patient safety safeguards are grounded in reproducible and trustworthy evidence. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251034690; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251034690
title: Reporting Gaps and Challenges in Randomized Trials of Generative AI for Medical Use: Insights From a Systematic Review

summary: Background: Digital media exposure is nearly universal by the preschool years. However, little is known about the timing of first exposure to different devices, and the factors associated with earlier exposure. Objective: This study examined age at first exposure to multiple digital devices and investigated sociodemographic, family, and behavioral factors associated with earlier exposure in preschool-aged children. We hypothesized that the timing of exposure would vary according to device-specific family and parental factors. Methods: Cross-sectional data from 892 Portuguese children aged 2 to 6 years were analyzed. Parents reported their children’s age at first exposure to television, video game consoles, computers, tablets, and smartphones. Children not yet exposed were treated as censored observations. Kaplan-Meier analyses estimated the median age at first exposure, and Cox proportional hazards models examined associations with child sex, parental education, parental screen time, and the presence of older siblings. Results: Among 892 children, exposure to digital devices was nearly universal (n=889, 99.7%), with television being the most common device. The median age at first exposure to any device was 12 months, with 581 (65.1%) children exposed by this age. Timing of exposure varied substantially across devices, with the earliest exposure observed for television, followed by smartphones and tablets, whereas computers and video game consoles were introduced later. Associations with earlier exposure differed by device. Earlier video game exposure was associated with being male and having older siblings. Parental screen time was statistically associated with earlier exposure to computers and tablets, although the magnitude of these associations was small. Smartphone exposure was associated with higher paternal education. No consistent factors were observed for television or overall device exposure. Conclusions: Digital device exposure begins during infancy and is widespread by the preschool years, but the timing and associated factors differ across devices. These findings suggest that early digital exposure is not a uniform behavior and support the importance of considering device-specific patterns when examining children’s early media experiences.
title: Determinants of Age at First Exposure to Digital Devices Among Children Aged 2 to 6 Years: Survival Analysis
